newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu on first Russia trip as Israel's leader.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu on first Russia trip as Israel's leader.

text.p: Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu embarked on Monday on his first trip to Russia since becoming prime minister nine months ago, planning to urge Moscow not to arm Israel's arch-foes Iran and Syria.
Russia, hoping to increase its Middle East peacemaking role, will host Netanyahu for 48 hours after a similar trip by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat last month.

Netanyahu will emphasise "Israel's growing concerns about the transfer of advanced military technologies to rogue states in the Middle East such as Iran -- Syria as well," his foreign policy adviser Dore Gold told Reuters.

Last month the Los Angeles Times said U.S. intelligence reports indicated Russia had given Iran technology for the Russian SS-4 missile, which has a range almost three times greater than that of any missile now in Tehran's arsenal.
Netanyahu said last week he would press Russia not to help Iran develop ballistic missiles. Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov denied the report.

Also on the trip, Netanyahu is expected to discuss the purchase of natural gas from Russia. Israel has been keen to diversify its energy sources and Gold said: "Obviously the energy issue is of tremendous interest."

Netanyahu, 47, will meet the 66-year-old President Boris Yeltsin, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Primakov along with Russian businessmen and the Moscow Jewish community before completing his trip in St Petersburg.

More than 650,000 Jews have moved to Israel from the former Soviet Union since Moscow flung open the doors to emigration in 1989 in an era of glasnost or openness, and Netanyahu's government has several prominent former Russians.

Former Soviet Jewish dissident Natan Sharansky is his trade minister, Yuli Edelstein is immigration minister, and the director-general of the prime minister's office is a former Russian, Avigdor Lieberman.

"Yeltsin will find a government that is well-versed in the Russian perspective and capable of developing a productive dialogue if the other side is willing to pursue it with the same interest," Gold said.
Moscow re-established long-severed ties with Israel only in 1991 for the launch of Arab-Israeli peace talks in Madrid co-sponsored by the United States and the then-Soviet Union.
It hopes to recover some of the Middle East clout it has lost because of economic woes.

Despite an apparent stalemate in their peace talks, Israeli and Palestinian officials expect Moscow to host multinational Middle East peace talks in late March that will include the United States, Russia and the European Union.

The late Yitzhak Rabin made the first visit of an Israeli prime minister to Moscow in 1994. Sharansky returned in January on his first trip since being freed from a KGB jail and turned over to the West in a dramatic prisoner swap in 1986.
Israeli officials say trade between the two countries, virtually non-existent five years ago, is now worth about $500 million a year and expanding fast.
